```json
      "category": "style",
      "title": "Stray empty JSDoc comment `/** */` above the handler",
      "body": "Line 16 contains `/** */` — an empty JSDoc block left over from development. It should be removed or replaced with a real description of the endpoint (method, auth, payload)."
    }
  ]
}
```

findings.title: Webhook secret comparison is not constant-time and fails open on missing env vars
findings.body: The webhook secret check uses a plain `!==` string comparison between `req.headers[...]` and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. This is vulnerable to timing attacks, and worse: if `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset (empty string) and the attacker sends an empty/missing header value, `undefined !== undefined` is false, so the check passes and the endpoint proceeds. Although `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` (packages/lib/constants.ts:103) requires both `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` and `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` to be truthy, the header lookup `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]` can still be `undefined` while the env var is set, and `undefined !== "secret"` correctly rejects — but the comparison should use a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual) and explicitly reject when either side is missing. Additionally, the endpoint does not restrict `req.method` to POST, so any HTTP method (GET, etc.) is accepted.

findings.title: Unhandled Zod parse error returns a 500 with stack details instead of a 400
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError when the body is invalid. In a Next.js API route, an uncaught throw results in a 500 response and potentially leaks validation error details (including the shape of expected fields) to the caller. It should be wrapped in `safeParse` and return a 400 with a generic message. The same applies to the `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` on line 57, which throws on malformed ciphertext or invalid JSON, producing an unhandled 500.

findings.title: Decryption uses an empty-string fallback key and stores arbitrary attacker-controlled JSON as credential key
findings.body: `symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")` falls back to an empty string if the env var is missing. Depending on the implementation of `symmetricDecrypt` in @calcom/lib/crypto, an empty key may either throw or (worse) be accepted, and the decrypted value is passed to `JSON.parse` with no schema validation before being written directly into `prisma.credential.key` (lines 78 and 85). A caller with the webhook secret could store arbitrary JSON structures as a credential, corrupting app behavior (e.g. missing `access_token`/`refresh_token` fields, wrong types). The decrypted `keys` should be validated against a zod schema (e.g. requiring `access_token: string`, `refresh_token: string`, `expiry_date: number`) before persisting, and the encryption key must be required (fail closed) rather than defaulting to `""`.

findings.title: TOCTOU race between findFirst and create can create duplicate credentials
findings.body: The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and then either `update` or `create` based on the result. Two concurrent webhook calls for the same user+app can both observe no existing credential and both execute `create`, producing duplicate credentials for the same user/app pair. Several app services assume a single credential per user (e.g. office365video callback deletes duplicates because 'when creating a video room we only do findFirst so if they have more than 1 others get ignored'), so duplicates silently break token refresh for the ignored rows. The lookup+write should be atomic (e.g. a transaction with serializable isolation, or a DB-level unique constraint plus upsert-style retry).

findings.title: Credential sync endpoint is called over plain fetch with no authentication, TLS validation is implicit, and the response is trusted blindly
findings.body: When `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set, `refreshOAuthTokens` POSTs `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` to that endpoint and returns the raw `Response`. There is no authentication on this outbound call (no shared secret header), so any party that can influence DNS/network could impersonate the endpoint; conversely the endpoint receives the userId in plaintext. More importantly, callers then treat the response body as valid OAuth tokens. In `parseRefreshTokenResponse` the `minimumTokenResponseSchema` only requires `access_token: z.string()` plus a numeric field — it does not require an expiry field, and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` then fabricates `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` (line 26) when absent. The fabricated refresh token is persisted to the DB (e.g. googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97-101 writes `key` including the fake refresh_token), which will permanently break future refreshes for that credential. The schema should require a real expiry and the code should refuse to persist a placeholder refresh token.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses invalid zod index-signature syntax and does not validate what callers need
findings.body: The schema declares `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. In zod, computed keys in object literals are not index signatures — `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to the literal string `"string"` (the result of `z.string().toString()`), so the schema effectively becomes `{ access_token: string, string: number, string: unknown }`, which is almost certainly not the intent and will mis-validate token responses (e.g. it may strip or reject real fields like `expires_in`). The intent was likely `.catchall(z.unknown())` or `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).passthrough()`. As written, when credential sharing is enabled the strict per-app schemas (e.g. `zoomRefreshedTokenSchema` requiring `refresh_token`, `expires_in`, `token_type`) are bypassed entirely, so malformed sync-endpoint responses are accepted and persisted.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is silently replaced with the literal string "refresh_token" and persisted
findings.body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — a placeholder string, not a token. Callers (e.g. packages/app-store/zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:118-124, packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:95-101) write this into `prisma.credential.key` and future refresh attempts will send `refresh_token="refresh_token"` to the provider, which will always fail with invalid_grant, permanently breaking the credential until the user reconnects. The correct behavior is to preserve the existing refresh token from the stored credential (OAuth providers typically omit refresh_token on refresh responses) or reject the response; writing a literal placeholder is a data-integrity bug.

findings.title: Token refresh reads `res?.data` but refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response whose body is never parsed in the sync path
findings.body: In the non-sync path, `refreshFunction` returns `fetchTokens.res` (a GaxiosResponse) and `res?.data` is the token JSON. But when credential sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `Response` object from `fetch(CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT)` (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8-15) — a `Response` has no `.data` property, so `token` is `undefined` and `token.access_token` on line 95 throws a TypeError. The sync path is therefore completely broken for Google Calendar: the code needs to `await response.json()` (and check `response.ok`) before reading `access_token`/`expiry_date`. The same mismatch affects every caller that expects the provider-shaped object: hubspot (expects a HubspotToken with `expiresIn`), lark (passes the Response into `handleLarkError` which calls `.json()` — that one works), office365 (`handleErrorsJson(response)` works), zoom/webex (`handleZoomResponse`/`handleWebexResponse` call `.json()` — work), but googlecalendar and hubspot and zoho-bigin and zohocrm and salesforce read `.data` directly and will crash or misbehave.

findings.title: HubSpot refresh treats a fetch Response as a HubspotToken, then reads `.expiresIn` off it
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `Response` object, but the code assigns it to `hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken` and immediately reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` (line 192) and `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken` (line 202). A `Response` has neither property, so `expiryDate` becomes `NaN` (`Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)`) and `setAccessToken(undefined)` is called, corrupting the stored credential with `expiryDate: NaN` and breaking all subsequent HubSpot calls. The response body must be parsed (`await response.json()`) and validated before use.

findings.title: zoho-bigin passes credentialId (a number) as the userId argument to refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes `credential.id` (the credential's primary key) where the function's third parameter is documented/used as `userId: number | null` and is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId` (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:11). The sync endpoint will therefore receive a credential ID instead of a Cal.com user ID, so the self-hoster's app store cannot map it to the right user and token refresh via sync will target the wrong (or no) user. It should pass `credential.userId` like every other integration does.

findings.title: Salesforce getClient performs a token refresh on every instantiation and never uses refreshOAuthTokens, and the new code has a logic bug in the error check
findings.body: The diff adds an unconditional `fetch` to Salesforce's token endpoint inside `getClient` (which runs in the constructor path for every calendar operation), so every Salesforce API call now triggers a refresh-token request — a performance regression and a behavioral change (Salesforce rotates refresh tokens; doing this per-request can invalidate tokens concurrently). Additionally, the guard `if (response.statusText !== "OK")` is wrong: `statusText` for a 200 response is typically `"OK"` but for many HTTP clients/proxies it can be empty; the correct check is `!response.ok`. As written, a successful response with an empty statusText would throw, and a failed response whose statusText happens to be "OK" would be treated as success. Also, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` is called but its result is checked with `accessTokenParsed.success` — however `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on failure and returns the safeParse result object on success, so `.success` works, but the earlier `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` after a throw is dead code; and the whole block ignores the credential-sync path entirely (no `refreshOAuthTokens` call), so Salesforce is not actually integrated with the sync feature despite the PR title.

findings.title: Salesforce credential update drops fields and uses prisma without import
findings.body: The added code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` at line 96, but `prisma` is not imported in this file (the imports at the top only include `@calcom/lib/*`, `@calcom/types/*`, and relative utils). This will be a `ReferenceError` at runtime (or a TS compile error) the first time a Salesforce client is constructed. Additionally, the update writes `key: { ...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token }`, discarding `instance_url` and other fields from the original credential that jsforce needs (the `new jsforce.Connection` below still reads `credentialKey.instance_url`, but the stored credential loses it on subsequent loads).

findings.title: Office365 refresh merges parsed token data but parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a safeParse result, and the old error logging was removed
findings.body: The code does `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) }`. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the zod safeParse result object (with `.success`/`.data`), so this spread is correct in shape — but note that when credential sync is enabled, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` validates against `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (which, per the schema bug, may strip fields) and fabricates `refresh_token: "refresh_token"`, which would overwrite the real refresh token in the stored credential. Also, the previous `console.error` logging of zod errors and the MS response was removed, so failures are now silent. And `refreshTokenResponseSchema` transforms `expires_in` into an absolute `expiry_date`-style value but the field is still named `expires_in` and `getToken` checks `isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)` — mixing semantics.

findings.title: MS Teams refresh computes expiry_date in milliseconds while isExpired compares against seconds-since-epoch elsewhere
findings.body: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)` produces milliseconds, and `isExpired = (expiryDate: number) => expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date())` compares against milliseconds too — so within this file it is consistent. However the credential is also written by `office365calendar/api/callback.ts` which sets `expiry_date = Math.round(+new Date() / 1000 + responseBody.expires_in)` (seconds). The two Office365 apps share the `msteams` app keys and the same `office365_video`/`office365_calendar` credential types are distinct, but any code path or future change that reads `expiry_date` with the other convention will misjudge expiry by a factor of 1000. At minimum this inconsistency between the two Office365 adapters (seconds in calendar callback/CalendarService, milliseconds in video adapter) is a latent bug; the units should be normalized and documented.

findings.title: isTokenValid logic is inverted
findings.body: `const isTokenValid = (token: ZoomToken) => (token.expires_in || token.expiry_date) < Date.now();` returns true when the token is expired (this is pre-existing code, unchanged by the diff, but the PR touches this file and the surrounding refresh logic). Combined with `getToken` returning the access token when `!isTokenValid(...)` is false, the naming/logic is inverted: `isTokenValid` actually means "is expired". This is confusing but functionally the refresh path triggers correctly; it is worth flagging because the PR modifies the refresh flow and a future refactor could easily flip it. (Pre-existing, but adjacent to changed lines 79-125.)

findings.title: parseRefreshTokenResponse result misused: it returns a safeParse result but the sync path bypasses zoomRefreshedTokenSchema
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled, `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema)` validates against `minimumTokenResponseSchema` instead of `zoomRefreshedTokenSchema`. The minimum schema only requires `access_token` and fabricates `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` when missing. Zoom's refresh response always includes a new `refresh_token`; if the sync endpoint omits it, the placeholder is persisted (line 120: `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`), permanently breaking Zoom token refresh. The code then reads `newTokens.expires_in` (line 122) which the minimum schema does not guarantee is present (its numeric catch-all is broken — see the parseRefreshTokenResponse finding), so `key.expiry_date` can become `NaN`.

findings.title: Webex isTokenValid logic is inverted (pre-existing, adjacent to changed refresh code)
findings.body: `const isTokenValid = (token: WebexToken) => token.expiry_date < Date.now();` returns true when the token is expired, and `getToken` uses `!isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve(credentialKey.access_token) : refreshAccessToken(...)`. Functionally this still refreshes when expired, but the inverted naming is a trap; the PR rewires the refresh path (lines 62-78) and any cleanup of this function could silently break refresh. Flagging because the changed code depends on this predicate.

findings.title: Zoho CRM isTokenValid logic is inverted (pre-existing, adjacent to changed refresh code)
findings.body: `const isValid = token && token.access_token && token.expiryDate && token.expiryDate < Date.now();` — this returns truthy when the token IS expired (expiryDate in the past), and `getToken` resolves without refreshing when `isTokenValid(credentialKey)` is true. So an expired token is treated as valid and the stale access token is used; a valid (unexpired) token triggers a refresh. This is inverted and will cause Zoho CRM calls to fail with 401 until the token happens to be refreshed by the other branch. The PR modifies the refresh function this predicate gates (lines 204-216), so the bug is directly in the changed feature's path.

findings.title: zoho-bigin expiryDate computed in milliseconds while BiginToken.expiryDate convention elsewhere is milliseconds — but isTokenValid compares to Date.now(), and the sync path returns a Response whose .data is undefined
findings.body: When sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `Response`; the code then reads `tokenInfo.data.error` (line 96) — a `Response` has no `.data`, so `tokenInfo.data` is `undefined` and `tokenInfo.data.error` throws a TypeError inside `refreshAccessToken`, which is not caught here (the function has no try/catch), so the whole auth fails. The non-sync path returns an axios response where `.data` is correct. The sync path must `await response.json()` first. (Same class of bug as the Google/HubSpot findings: callers assume provider-shaped objects but receive a fetch Response.)

findings.title: Lark refresh passes a fetch Response into handleLarkError which expects a Response — OK — but the sync path response is not JSON-validated and refresh token rotation is mishandled
findings.body: In the sync path, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `Response` from the sync endpoint; `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log)` presumably calls `resp.json()` and checks Lark's `code !== 0` envelope. A self-hoster's sync endpoint returning `{ access_token, expires_in, refresh_token, refresh_expires_in }` (flat, no Lark envelope) would fail the `code === 0` check or produce `data.data` undefined, throwing. The sync contract (flat token response) is incompatible with Lark's envelope expectations unless handleLarkError is tolerant. Additionally, when the sync endpoint does not return a new `refresh_token`, `newLarkAuthCredentials.refresh_token` becomes `undefined` and overwrites the stored refresh token (line 92), breaking future refreshes — the existing refresh token should be preserved when the response omits one.

findings.title: No timeout, no retry, and no Content-Type header on the sync endpoint request; response.ok is never checked
findings.body: The `fetch` to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` has no `AbortController`/timeout, so a hung sync endpoint will block token refresh indefinitely (calendar operations hang). There is no `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` header even though the body is `URLSearchParams` (some servers reject or misparse the body without it). And the returned `Response` is never checked for `ok`/status — a 500 from the sync endpoint is treated the same as a success and its body is parsed as tokens by callers, persisting garbage (e.g. an HTML error page fails JSON.parse, or a JSON error object is partially accepted by the broken minimum schema).

findings.title: Credential creation does not set `invalid: false` explicitly and does not validate that appMetadata.type matches the app's expected credential type
findings.body: When creating a credential, the handler uses `type: appMetadata.type` from `appStoreMetadata`. If the appSlug maps to an app whose metadata `type` differs from what the app's services expect (e.g. a slug collision or a misconfigured app store entry), the credential is created with a wrong `type`, and services that look up credentials by `type` (e.g. `findFirst({ where: { type: "zoom_video" } })`) will not find it. There is also no validation that the decrypted `keys` object contains the fields the app requires (access_token, refresh_token, expiry). The webhook should validate the payload shape per app type or at least a minimal common shape.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string-or-empty value, not a boolean, and is used in boolean contexts
findings.body: `export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` evaluates to `string | undefined` (the value of the last truthy env var, or `undefined`). It is used as a boolean in `if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)` (works) and in `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT)` (works), but exporting a truthy string as a flag named `..._ENABLED` is misleading and will break if anyone does strict `=== true` checks or serializes it. It should be wrapped in `Boolean(...)` or `!!(...)`.

findings.title: Unrelated hardcoded redirect URI change slipped into the diff
findings.body: The diff changes `const redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback`` to a hardcoded `` `/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback` ``. If `appConfig.slug` is `"zoho-bigin"` this is a no-op, but if the config slug ever differs (e.g. a renamed app), the OAuth redirect URI registered in Zoho would silently mismatch. This change is unrelated to the credential-sync feature and should either be reverted or justified.

findings.title: No tests for the new webhook endpoint or the sync/refresh helpers
findings.body: The PR adds a new public API endpoint (`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`) and two new shared helpers (`refreshOAuthTokens`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) that alter the token-refresh path of ~10 integrations, but the PR description's checklist explicitly states "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works". There are no unit tests covering: webhook secret validation, the disabled-feature 403, user/app lookup, decrypt+create/update, the sync-vs-direct branch in refreshOAuthTokens, or the placeholder refresh_token behavior in parseRefreshTokenResponse. Given that the refresh path is security-critical (OAuth tokens), tests are needed before merge.

findings.title: Inconsistent app slug values passed by different integrations ("zoomvideo" vs "zoom", "msteams" vs "office365-calendar")
findings.body: Callers pass different slug strings for the same underlying app: zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts passes `"zoomvideo"` while zoomvideo/api/callback.ts creates the credential with `appId: "zoom"`; office365video passes `"msteams"` while office365calendar passes `"office365-calendar"`. The sync endpoint receives `appSlug` and must map it to the self-hoster's app store; inconsistent slugs between the credential's `appId` and the sync request's `appSlug` will cause lookups to fail on the self-hoster side. The slug sent to the sync endpoint should match the credential's `appId` (i.e. `credential.appId`) rather than a hardcoded per-call-site string.

findings.title: parseRefreshTokenResponse return value used as the credential key, discarding the original credential fields
findings.body: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` — `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the zod safeParse result object (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed data. This `key` is then written to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })` (line 100). So the stored credential key becomes `{ success: true, data: { ...tokens } }` instead of the token object itself — the credential is corrupted and `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` on next load will fail (the stored object has no `access_token` at the top level). It should be `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data` (after checking `.success`). This is a direct data-corruption bug in the changed lines.

findings.title: parseRefreshTokenResponse return value spread includes the `success` flag into the credential key
findings.body: `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) }` — this correctly spreads only `.data`, so this call site is fine; however note that `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on failure, so `tokenResponse.success` is always true here and the `&&` guard is dead. Not a bug per se, but combined with the googlecalendar misuse of the same helper (returning the whole result object), the helper's return type (`SafeParseReturnType`) is error-prone: callers must remember to unwrap `.data`. The helper should either return the parsed data directly (throwing on failure, which it already does) or be renamed/typed to make the unwrapping explicit.

findings.title: Stray empty JSDoc comment `/** */` above the handler
findings.body: Line 16 contains `/** */` — an empty JSDoc block left over from development. It should be removed or replaced with a real description of the endpoint (method, auth, payload).
